profiles.summary: Audit support, axial organisation and breathing without relying on the picture or extra range.
profiles.prerequisite: Experience with basic yoga positions and an ability to choose rest independently.

profiles.summary: Distinguish spinal movement, pelvic movement and neck compensation through controlled comparison.
profiles.prerequisite: A repeatable baseline and a clear personal stop rule.

profiles.summary: Analyse standing support, hip hinging and balance recovery while keeping dependable support.
profiles.prerequisite: Comfort with supported standing and deliberate release.

profiles.summary: Manage leg, pelvis, trunk and arm cues together without trading comfort for a deeper shape.
profiles.prerequisite: Stable supported standing and the ability to explain two alignment priorities.

profiles.summary: Study how limb movement affects trunk control, leverage and the quality of an exit.
profiles.prerequisite: Comfort with the supplied floor preparations and wrist/knee supports.

profiles.summary: Compare small supported backbends, distinguishing distributed movement from local compression.
profiles.prerequisite: Comfortable small-range backbend experience; discuss uncertainty with a qualified teacher.

profiles.summary: Analyse hip position, pelvic movement and side differences without forcing symmetry or range.
profiles.prerequisite: An established habit of adapting positions and respecting side-to-side differences.

profiles.summary: Combine support, trunk organisation, controlled transitions and contingency planning.
profiles.prerequisite: Reliable use of support and an exit plan before each balance attempt.

profiles.summary: Analyse arm-balance, shoulder and kneeling preparation through observation and teacher discussion.
profiles.prerequisite: Bring prior notes and questions to a qualified teacher. App progress does not establish readiness.
competencies: Differentiate preparation from a full skill

profiles.summary: Defend an individualised sequence, adaptations and coaching decisions in a teacher-guided capstone.
profiles.prerequisite: Qualified teacher participation for readiness decisions and any advanced progression.
competencies: Adapt a sequence to a case

g01: Support before effort
In easy seat, identify which contacts support your weight and which muscles you are unnecessarily bracing. Explain one support change using the supplied cues.
Your seated posture looks upright, but your jaw and shoulders are braced. What is the better next experiment?
Adjust support and reduce unnecessary effort.
Brace harder to keep the outline exact.
Extend the attempt until tension disappears.
A visual outline does not establish useful control. Change support or effort, then observe comfort.
A one-variable comparison
Compare your usual seat with one comfortable support adjustment. Keep the task brief; describe what changed in effort rather than which looked more advanced.
What makes a support comparison interpretable?
Change one factor and record its effect.
Change height, leg position and breathing together.
Choose the position with the deepest shape.
One changed factor makes the observation easier to interpret; appearance is not the outcome.
Reconstruct the seated setup
Without looking at the cue list, explain setup, an alignment priority, a release and a fallback. Then reopen the cues and identify a missing detail.
A recall exercise reveals a missing release step. What should you do?
Review and include a controlled exit before attempting.
Treat entry as sufficient preparation.
Use a longer hold to memorise the setup.
Recall tests understanding, not endurance. Release and fallback are part of the plan.
Standing baseline audit
For Mountain, distinguish foot contact, knee softness and shoulder effort. Name which observation comes from sensation and which only from an image.
Which report separates observation from assumption?
I notice foot pressure; a teacher would need to assess my alignment.
The illustration proves my joints are aligned.
Standing still proves readiness for advanced balances.
Sensory observations and visual examples are different kinds of evidence.
Two-cue attention
During a brief optional Mountain attempt, attend to even weight and soft knees together. If attention becomes strained, simplify rather than increasing duration.
A second cue makes you stiffen and hold your breath. How should the task change?
Return to one cue or rest.
Keep both cues and suppress the urge to breathe.
Add a third cue to improve concentration.
Difficulty comes from clear attention; excessive bracing is a reason to simplify.
Explain the trade-off
Defend a comfortable standing modification. State what it helps you notice and what the illustration cannot tell you about your own readiness.
Why can a supported modification be a demanding technical choice?
It can isolate a specific learning objective.
It automatically proves the original pose is mastered.
It must be removed before a grade can be completed.
Support can make a technical question more precise without making a mastery claim.
Rest as an observable skill
Study bent-knee rest. Identify a comfortable setup, a sign of unnecessary effort and the release sequence. Compare resting with merely freezing in place.
Which observation best fits recovery?
Breathing is unforced and I can change position comfortably.
I remain perfectly still regardless of discomfort.
A longer rest makes later positions compulsory.
Comfortable recovery allows movement and choice; stillness is not the goal by itself.
Design a transition on paper
Write the stages for leaving bent-knee rest using the supplied release cue. Identify where you would pause and how you would avoid rushing.
What belongs in an exit plan from bent-knee rest?
A side roll before slowly sitting up, if comfortable.
A fast sit-up to test strength.
A rule to remain still until the next clock checkpoint.
The supplied exit uses a side roll and a gradual return; the schedule is not a movement command.
Cross-position cue audit
Compare easy seat, Mountain and rest: identify a shared breathing principle and a support requirement that changes. Defend why one cue cannot describe all three setups.
Which principle transfers across these three positions?
Normal unforced breathing, with position-specific support.
Identical joint angles in every position.
Continuous abdominal bracing in every position.
A shared breathing principle does not erase differences in support and position.
Foundation case defence
Create a written three-position learning plan with setup, one technical objective per position, a fallback and a release. Include a reason to repeat this grade.
What would justify repeating this grade?
A useful question or an inconsistent setup remains.
Only an incomplete clock window.
A failure to reach a prescribed stretch depth.
Repeating can address uncertainty; time and depth do not establish readiness.
g02: Neutral is an investigation
Audit Tabletop using the written neutral-spine cue. Identify the mild extension in the illustration and explain why copying it exactly may miss the learning objective.
The Tabletop image and written neutral cue differ. Which takes priority for this draft lesson?
The written cue and qualified teacher review.
The image because every generated detail is validated.
Whichever shape requires the greatest effort.
The kit explicitly flags mild extension in this image; it is a draft reference.
Contact and substitution
Map hand and knee support in Tabletop. Explain how a support or padding change could affect your ability to notice trunk effort without prescribing a larger range.
Wrist discomfort disrupts your attention. What is the next step?
Release and choose support, rest or teacher guidance.
Shift more weight onto the wrists to adapt faster.
Ignore it if the trunk remains steady.
Discomfort is a stop signal, not a concentration challenge.
Neutral return from memory
Describe an entry, a comfortable neutral reference and an exit for Tabletop. Distinguish a repeatable reference from a rigid fixed shape.
What makes a neutral reference useful?
It can be found comfortably without excessive bracing.
It exactly matches the atlas pixels.
It prevents any spinal movement afterward.
A reference is useful for comparison and comfort, not for rigid imitation.
Cat: locate the movement
Read the Cat cues and describe where the intended gentle rounding occurs. Identify a way that forcing the neck could imitate movement without answering the spinal-control task.
Which response to a small comfortable rounding is appropriate?
Accept the available range and keep the neck unforced.
Pull the chin down to make the curve larger.
Repeat until the shape matches the picture exactly.
The supplied cue asks for gentle rounding without forcing the neck.
Separate sequence from speed
Explain the order of a gentle Cat exploration and return to neutral. During an optional window, prioritise a deliberate start and release over repetitions.
How is movement quality assessed in this mission?
By a deliberate comfortable sequence and clear observations.
By the number of cycles completed before the timer ends.
By how quickly the spine reaches the illustration.
This mission tests sequence and control; the trial cap is not a repetition target.
Identify a compensating cue
Compare the intended Cat cue with an exaggerated instruction such as pulling the head down. Explain which information would help a teacher distinguish the two.
Which note gives the teacher useful evidence?
Where movement was noticed and what felt strained.
Only the number of completed checkpoints.
A claim that the picture and body look identical.
A concrete observation is more informative than a completion count or an assumed visual match.
Cow: keep the neck question open
Analyse the Cow illustration against its long-neck review note. Explain how lifting the chin can change the picture without proving appropriate spinal movement.
The picture lifts the chin. What does the review note ask you to consider?
A long comfortable neck rather than copying the chin lift.
A stronger backward neck tilt.
A breath hold to maintain the head position.
The specific art review flags the chin position for instructor review.
Compare Cat and Cow priorities
Contrast the two written alignment cues and locate the shared neutral return. Avoid using the size of either curve as a performance score.
Which comparison is technically useful?
How each movement returns to a comfortable neutral reference.
Which produces the largest visible curve.
Which can be held longest without resting.
A controlled reference and return provide useful learning evidence without encouraging extra range.
Design a regression decision
Write a decision tree for a Cat/Cow lesson: comfortable, uncertain, and uncomfortable. Assign a smaller task, observation or rest to the appropriate branch.
Uncertainty about where movement occurs should lead to what?
Simplification or observation and a teacher question.
More force to make the movement obvious.
Automatic advancement after the hour ends.
Uncertainty is a learning question, not a reason to intensify or advance automatically.
Spinal-control case study
Prepare a written explanation of Tabletop, Cat and Cow for a teacher. Include image limitations, support choices, movement distinctions and release options.
What would demonstrate stronger understanding of this grade?
Explaining movement differences and the limits of the images.
Claiming to diagnose spinal alignment from the atlas.
Performing the deepest possible backbend.
The capstone is an evidence-based explanation; it is not an anatomical assessment.
g03: Hinge or collapse?
Analyse the chair-supported half-fold. Distinguish the intended supported hip hinge from reaching lower merely to deepen the outline.
Which goal best matches a supported half-fold analysis?
Understand the hinge and support relationship.
Reach a lower target at any cost.
Remove the chair before learning the setup.
The support is part of the task and can clarify where movement is organised.
Support placement reasoning
Explain how you would check that the chair is stable before a brief attempt. Describe a support-related uncertainty you would bring to a teacher.
Which condition should be addressed before using a chair?
The support is stable and the space is clear.
The chair looks like the illustration.
The next scheduled checkpoint has arrived.
Appearance and clock time cannot establish a stable support.
Half-fold teach-back
Describe setup, a comfortable range choice and an exit for the supported half-fold without looking. Compare your explanation with the supplied cues.
A technically strong teach-back includes what?
Entry, support, a learning priority and an exit.
Only the final outline.
A fixed depth that everyone must achieve.
A movement explanation needs context and an exit, not just a shape.
Heel raise: map the load
For a supported heel raise, explain the role of dependable support and describe what you would observe during rising and lowering without adding repetition targets.
What is the role of support in this heel-raise mission?
It supports a controlled comparison of rising and lowering.
It must be removed to make the lesson count.
It guarantees balance readiness.
Support permits analysis; it is not a readiness guarantee or a grading penalty.
The lowering phase
Use the written heel-raise cues to explain a deliberate lowering and a rest option. Compare controlling the return with simply reaching the top position.
Which phase belongs in a complete heel-raise analysis?
Both the rise and a controlled comfortable return.
Only the highest point.
Only the number of repetitions.
A complete task includes the return and the option to rest.
Change one demand
Design an off-mat comparison that changes one attentional demand while retaining support. State why adding height, speed and repetitions together would obscure the result.
Why should several demands not be increased at once?
It becomes difficult to identify what caused a change.
It makes the exercise automatically unsafe in all cases.
It prevents the app from counting checkpoints.
The reasoning task is to isolate the effect of a change, not to infer readiness from a count.
Tree preparation: plan the exit
Analyse wall-tree preparation. Describe the support, foot-placement limits in the supplied cue and a simple route back to a stable stance.
When should the balance exit be decided?
Before a brief attempt begins.
Only after balance is lost.
After the clock moves to the next checkpoint.
Preparing a route out is part of the setup rather than a response to the schedule.
Balance evidence
Compare a comfortable supported side with the other side without forcing equal performance. Record the difference and a support decision.
What is the best interpretation of a side difference?
A reason to adapt and discuss, not force symmetry.
Proof of a diagnosis.
A reason to repeat the weaker side until it matches.
A difference is an observation; it does not diagnose a cause or justify forcing the other side.
A support-preserving challenge
Increase the technical demand by tracking breath, contact and exit readiness together. Retain support and simplify if attention disrupts comfort.
How can this mission become more demanding without removing support?
Coordinate several observations while preserving comfort.
Close the eyes and remove support.
Stand until fatigue forces an exit.
Attention and decision complexity can increase while support and short windows remain.
Standing strategy capstone
Write a supported-standing lesson linking a hinge, a heel raise and tree preparation. Give each a distinct purpose, support check and fallback.
Which capstone plan is most defensible?
A plan with distinct goals, supports and exits.
A plan that removes every support by the end.
A plan that equates a finished hour with balance mastery.
Planning quality is demonstrated by clear reasoning, not by mandatory removal of support.
g04: Warrior II priorities
Identify the leg and arm alignment priorities in Warrior II. Explain which cue you would simplify first if attending to both creates excessive effort.
When two cues compete with comfort, what should lead?
Reduce task complexity and use a comfortable range.
Deepen the stance to make both cues more obvious.
Hold the breath while arranging the arms.
Managing competing priorities includes knowing when to simplify.
Stance comparison
Describe a one-variable comparison between comfortable stance choices. Evaluate control and breathing rather than depth or resemblance to the artwork.
What should a stance comparison evaluate?
Comfort, control and breathing within the available range.
The widest distance between the feet.
How much muscular shaking appears.
More demanding reasoning does not require a wider or more fatiguing stance.
Explain both sides
Prepare bilateral cue notes for Warrior II. State what transfers between sides and what may need individual adaptation without mirroring the illustration.
What should remain flexible across sides?
The support and range chosen for comfort.
The requirement to match both sides exactly.
The instruction to keep going through pain.
The illustration is fixed; bilateral learning requires side-specific judgement.
Side angle support strategy
Analyse the supported side-angle setup. Explain how support can clarify trunk and leg organisation instead of being treated as a shortcut.
What does a block or other supplied support change?
The conditions of the learning task, not its legitimacy.
The need to breathe normally.
The stop rule for discomfort.
Support can change the task while normal breathing and stop rules still apply.
Trunk versus reach
Separate a comfortable trunk organisation from the desire to reach farther in side angle. Describe how you would notice a reach that disrupts control.
A farther reach disrupts your breathing. Which observation matters most?
The reach has exceeded the useful task for now.
The larger outline proves improved technique.
The timer requires the reach to be maintained.
Breathing and comfort take priority over an expanded outline.
Prioritisation case
Explain how you would choose between adjusting stance, using more support and observing a side-angle lesson. Defend the choice using a concrete observation.
Which choice is appropriate when the setup remains uncertain?
Observe and ask a teacher rather than adding demand.
Remove the support to make the decision simpler.
Assume attendance verifies the alignment.
Uncertainty remains a valid reason for observation or teacher input.
Triangle: distinguish reach from hinge
Study triangle with a block. Explain the role of the block and the difference between a comfortable hinge and chasing a lower hand position.
What should determine the block-supported hand position?
A comfortable setup that serves the learning goal.
The lowest available block height.
The hand position of the generated character.
A draft image is not an individual range prescription.
Three-plane observation
List observations about stance, trunk orientation and arm effort in triangle. Identify which observations you can report and which require teacher assessment.
Which claim exceeds what this app can establish?
The image proves my three-dimensional alignment is correct.
I noticed effort in my shoulders.
I used a higher support comfortably.
Static artwork cannot establish your individual three-dimensional alignment.
Contrast three standing patterns
Compare Warrior II, side angle and triangle. Identify one shared priority and one cue that must change rather than applying a single instruction to all three.
What is the value of contrasting these standing positions?
It reveals where cues transfer and where they differ.
It produces a single universal joint-angle target.
It removes the need for individual modifications.
Technical understanding includes the boundaries of a cue, not only its repetition.
Standing precision defence
Defend a written standing sequence, including a side-specific modification, a support choice, a transition plan and a reason to stop.
Which outcome belongs to this capstone?
A defensible sequence and clear limits, pending teacher review.
An automatic advanced-readiness certificate.
A requirement for deeper ranges in every pose.
This is a planning assessment; it cannot certify a body’s readiness.
g05: Bird dog: trunk or limb?
Analyse bird dog by separating limb reach from trunk substitution. Explain how a smaller reach can make the technical task more precise.
A longer reach turns into trunk rotation. Which experiment is more informative?
Shorten the reach and observe trunk organisation.
Reach farther to compensate.
Extend the trial until rotation disappears.
A smaller lever can clarify the intended control task.
Contralateral attention
Describe the relationship between opposite limbs in the supplied bird-dog setup. Track a stable support contact and an unforced breath during a brief optional attempt.
What makes a contralateral task technically demanding?
Coordinating limb action with trunk and support awareness.
Performing it as fast as possible.
Maximising limb height.
Coordination and observation, rather than speed or height, define this task.
Regression reasoning
Write a regression for bird dog using a smaller task or observation. Explain what evidence would make you retain the simpler version.
When should a regression remain useful?
When it allows a clearer comfortable learning task.
Only until a fixed number of checkpoints is finished.
Only when a user is a beginner.
Experienced practitioners can use regressions to answer precise technical questions.
Knees-down plank audit
Read the plank illustration’s lumbar-extension review note. Explain how rib and pelvis organisation differs from holding the pictured outline.
Why does the plank review note matter?
The generated outline needs alignment review rather than literal imitation.
It authorises an unsupported full plank.
It means a longer hold is required.
The supplied illustration has a specific limitation; it does not prescribe a progression.
Load and breath
Compare contact, trunk effort and breathing in the supplied knees-down preparation. Plan a release before attempting; rest if effort overwhelms normal breathing.
Breathing becomes strained in the preparation. Which response is appropriate?
Release and reduce demand or observe.
Continue until the trial timer expires.
Hold the breath to stabilise the trunk.
The optional window is a maximum opportunity, not a requirement to maintain effort.
Leverage case study
Explain to a teacher how changing a lever can change a trunk-control task. Use the supplied knees-down version as your reference rather than unlocking a harder pose.
What does understanding leverage establish?
A basis for discussion, not automatic permission for a harder variation.
Proof that the full variation is safe for everyone.
A reason to double the trial duration.
A reasoning answer is not a physical readiness assessment.
Boat preparation: choose the task
Analyse bent-knee boat preparation. Distinguish a useful support-and-trunk task from pursuing a dramatic leg or torso position.
Which target is appropriate for this boat-preparation mission?
A comfortable controlled preparation with a planned release.
The most extended leg shape available.
The longest hold you can tolerate.
The supplied preparation is the reference; extending the shape is not compulsory.
Controlled entry and exit
Explain how you would enter and leave boat preparation without using momentum as a substitute for control. Record an observable sign that the task needs simplification.
Which sign supports simplifying a task?
Rushing or momentum replaces a deliberate entry.
The pose looks less dramatic than the illustration.
Another grade has been browsed.
A loss of deliberateness is relevant evidence; appearance and browsing are not.
Three trunk-control comparisons
Compare bird dog, knees-down plank and boat preparation by support pattern and limb leverage. Explain why identical effort cues may not fit all three.
Why compare support patterns?
They change the coordination and leverage questions.
They give a universal exertion score.
They allow the app to verify muscle activation.
The app cannot measure muscle activation or derive a universal physical difficulty score.
Coordination capstone
Defend a written trunk-control lesson with one regression per preparation, normal-breathing priorities and deliberate exits. Identify what a teacher still needs to assess.
What remains outside the app’s assessment?
Individual physical readiness and alignment verification.
Whether a written answer was selected correctly.
Whether a note was saved.
Knowledge checks and saved notes do not establish individual physical readiness.
g06: Sphinx support analysis
Analyse Sphinx using the supplied small-range cues. Distinguish a comfortable supported position from chasing greater spinal extension.
Which target serves this Sphinx mission?
A supported comfortable range with unforced breathing.
The largest visible arch.
A fixed amount of spinal extension for everyone.
The task is discrimination and support, not maximum range.
Distribution versus compression
Describe the difference between a distributed movement intention and a focal sensation of compression. Treat uncertainty as a teacher question rather than a reason to push.
A focal uncomfortable sensation appears. What should happen?
Release and rest; discuss it with a qualified teacher.
Increase the arch to spread the movement.
Wait for the next checkpoint before changing position.
Uncomfortable sensations call for stopping, not for attempting to solve them with more range.
Support trade-off defence
Explain the support role in Sphinx and a reason to choose observation. State what you can notice yourself and what the static image cannot verify.
Which statement respects the image’s limits?
I can report comfort; the image cannot assess my body.
Matching the picture proves safe extension.
The generated artwork is clinically validated.
The artwork is an unreviewed illustration, not an individual assessment.
Low cobra: effort direction
Read the low-cobra cues and describe a small deliberate exploration. Distinguish the intention to organise the trunk from pushing into a larger outline.
Which change would miss the purpose of this mission?
Using more force simply to create a higher outline.
Choosing a smaller comfortable exploration.
Writing down a question for a teacher.
The mission asks for technical discrimination, not a higher shape.
Breathing as feedback
Explain how normal breathing informs a small low-cobra learning task. If attention to the cue changes breathing or comfort, simplify or observe.
How should strained breathing be used?
As a reason to release or reduce task demand.
As proof that a useful challenge has begun.
As a cue to hold the breath deliberately.
The curriculum retains normal unforced breathing and the ability to stop.
Sphinx–cobra comparison
Contrast the support arrangements and learning priorities of Sphinx and low cobra. Explain why one illustration cannot define the other setup.
A useful comparison should focus on what?
Different support arrangements and written priorities.
Which backbend reaches the greatest height.
Which permits the longest continuous hold.
Comparing support and priorities tests understanding without encouraging extra range.
Low bridge: setup logic
Analyse low bridge using its supplied setup and release cues. Write how you would check a comfortable base before any brief exploration.
Which belongs before an optional low-bridge attempt?
A comfortable setup and a clear release plan.
A target for maximum height.
A requirement to complete the entire timer.
Setup and release precede an optional attempt; height and duration are not the goal.
Exit control
Describe a deliberate release from low bridge, including what would lead you to stop earlier. Separate a controlled exit from the size of the lift.
What is evidence of a more considered exit?
An intentional comfortable release that can happen early.
Maintaining the lift until the bell regardless of comfort.
A visibly larger arch before releasing.
The ability to leave deliberately is a distinct learning objective.
Three extension strategies
Compare Sphinx, low cobra and low bridge by contacts, support and release. Write one uncertainty for each without prescribing a progression into deep backbends.
What follows from completing these comparisons?
A stronger discussion basis, not permission for deep backbends.
Automatic readiness for a full backbend.
A requirement to intensify the next day.
Completion does not unlock deep backbends or establish readiness.
Extension case defence
Build a written case in which a smaller range is the better technical choice. Defend supports, normal breathing, rest and the need for qualified feedback.
Which justification is technically strongest?
The smaller range permits a clearer comfortable objective.
It allows more checkpoints to be completed rapidly.
It guarantees clinical benefit.
A clear objective and honest limits make a stronger argument than counts or treatment claims.
g07: Butterfly: support and rotation
Analyse supported butterfly. Explain how support and comfortable hip position matter more than lowering the knees to match the image.
Which goal would undermine this mission?
Forcing the knees downward to match the illustration.
Using support to stay comfortable.
Reporting a difference between sides.
The generated shape is not an individual range target.
Separate motion sources
Distinguish intended hip movement from compensating movement elsewhere in a butterfly setup. Name a question that requires teacher observation.
What can your written report establish?
Your observations and uncertainties, not a diagnosis.
A precise anatomical explanation for every sensation.
A universal correction for other learners.
A self-report is evidence for discussion, not a diagnosis or universal prescription.
Adaptation defence
Explain why a supported or smaller butterfly position may be technically appropriate for an experienced practitioner. Specify the learning question it serves.
When is a support-based adaptation legitimate?
Whenever it serves a clear comfortable objective.
Only before someone has tried the original shape.
Only if both knees reach the same height.
Experience does not remove the value of support or require symmetry.
Figure four: pelvic substitution
Study reclined figure four and distinguish hip positioning from changing the trunk or pelvis just to deepen the outline. Use the supplied comfort limits.
What should lead a figure-four comparison?
Comfort and clarity about the intended task.
The deepest possible shape.
The closest visual match to the character.
The goal is useful discrimination within individual limits.
Bilateral evidence
Record separate observations for each side of figure four. Explain why using different comfortable supports may be more defensible than forcing equal ranges.
What does a side difference require?
A documented adaptation or teacher question.
An automatic diagnosis.
Equal practice through discomfort.
Side differences invite adaptation and discussion rather than forced matching.
Support decision case
Create a figure-four case where the user chooses observation. State the uncertain variable and a precise question for the teacher.
Which teacher question is most useful?
How can this setup be adapted to the discomfort I noticed?
Can I ignore discomfort to match the other side?
Does completing the timer verify my hip alignment?
A specific observation and adaptation question support a useful discussion.
Low lunge: organise the base
Analyse padded low lunge. Explain the role of knee padding and a comfortable stance before discussing reach or depth.
Which condition should be addressed first?
A comfortable supported base.
Maximum forward reach.
Removing padding to increase difficulty.
The support and comfort conditions remain part of an experienced technical task.
Hip motion versus extra depth
Compare a comfortable low-lunge objective with an instruction to sink farther. Explain which observations might show that extra depth is obscuring the task.
What would justify reducing range?
The extra depth disrupts comfort or organisation.
The supported version looks simpler.
The next grade is available.
A useful range serves the objective and comfort; it is not selected by appearance.
Three hip contexts
Contrast butterfly, figure four and low lunge by support, side differences and release. Identify why the same range cue cannot be imposed on all three.
Why should range cues remain specific to the position?
The positions and support conditions differ.
The app can measure exact hip rotation.
Every learner should eventually reach identical angles.
Different conditions call for specific reasoning; the app does not measure anatomy.
Adaptation dossier
Prepare a written case with separate side observations, support options and a stop/rest decision for each pose. Include what still needs qualified review.
What is the best evidence of learning here?
A clear adaptation rationale and honest uncertainty.
Identical bilateral range.
A claim that the generated artwork validates your joints.
The dossier assesses reasoning and observation rather than physical symmetry.
g08: Chair: competing demands
Analyse shallow chair with the supplied comfortable range. Coordinate stance, trunk effort and breathing without treating depth as the challenge score.
How should chair difficulty be approached in this mission?
Through coordinated priorities in a comfortable shallow task.
By increasing depth until fatigue appears.
By holding until the timer finishes.
The technical demand is coordination, not compulsory depth or fatigue.
Transition intention
Explain a deliberate entry to and exit from shallow chair. Identify where rushing could conceal uncertainty and how you would simplify.
What makes a transition more technically useful?
A clear controlled entry and exit with a fallback.
Speed between shapes.
Eliminating every pause.
A transition is a learning task, not a race.
Two-condition comparison
Plan an off-mat comparison of a familiar chair setup and one small comfortable adjustment. State the single question and what evidence would answer it.
What belongs in a comparison plan?
One question, one change and a way to describe the result.
Several changes and a maximum-effort target.
A promise of a specific physical improvement.
An interpretable comparison is specific and does not promise an outcome.
Supported Warrior III strategy
Study supported Warrior III. Explain support contact, trunk intention and the exit before considering any optional attempt.
Which instruction fits the supported reference?
Keep dependable support and pre-plan the exit.
Remove support to make the attempt count.
Stay until balance fails.
The support is integral to the supplied preparation.
Control without lever escalation
Increase the attentional challenge by tracking contact, breathing and trunk organisation together. Keep the supplied supported form and simplify if control is lost.
What is a suitable technical escalation?
Coordinate more observations without forcing a harder shape.
Maximise lever length regardless of control.
Add a blindfold or unstable support.
The challenge is integration of observations while retaining a dependable setup.
Balance contingency case
Write a decision plan for uncertainty during supported Warrior III. Include release, rest and a question that a teacher could answer by observation.
If balance becomes uncertain, what should lead?
Use the planned release and regain a comfortable base.
Stay in place to prove commitment.
Wait for the notification before changing position.
The exit plan and comfort take priority over a clock or achievement goal.
Dancer preparation: support logic
Analyse supported dancer preparation as supplied. Explain why it remains a preparation and why additional reach is not established by completing earlier grades.
What does finishing Grade 7 establish for dancer preparation?
Learning history, not permission for a deeper variation.
Verified readiness for an unsupported balance.
A requirement to increase the backbend.
A prior grade count does not assess individual physical readiness.
Multi-priority rehearsal
Mentally rehearse support, comfortable range, normal breathing and exit for dancer preparation. Identify the priority that becomes unclear first.
What should happen when one priority becomes unclear?
Simplify the task or observe and ask a teacher.
Increase effort to make the shape more stable.
Ignore that priority until the timer ends.
Recognising the limit of attention is part of technical judgement.
Compare recovery strategies
Compare the route out of chair, supported Warrior III and dancer preparation. Explain which recovery choices can transfer and which depend on the pose.
Why compare exits across balances?
It develops contingency reasoning specific to each setup.
It makes falls a required learning outcome.
It proves that all balances share one exit.
Exit reasoning is specific; falling is not a required exercise.
Integration capstone
Design a written supported-balance lesson with paired priorities, one-variable comparisons, recoveries and a readiness question for a teacher.
What is the strongest capstone conclusion?
I can explain a plan and identify what still needs review.
The app verified my balance technique.
I must remove supports next time.
A technical plan remains distinct from instructor verification or compulsory progression.
g09: Dolphin readiness observation
